activities.caption: the artist says: 'I meant it' — what weighs?
activities.name: critIntentBranch

config.root: In a crit, the painter says the painting was meant to feel lonely. The room must decide what counts as evidence.

choices.label: The stated intention — the artist was there
choices.feedback: The intentional fallacy (Wimsatt and Beardsley) says no: 'I meant it to feel lonely' is not evidence the painting achieves loneliness.

choices.label: The work's actual devices — empty centre, cold palette, cropped figure
choices.feedback: Work-first: the devices are observable, arguable and testable — the critique's evidence.

choices.label: Whether you personally felt lonely looking at it
choices.feedback: A data point, but the work-first rule asks for features, not feelings — a verdict with no observable features attached cannot be tested or taught.

intent.text: Defending or accepting intentions changes nothing on the wall — the artist need not defend, and the critiquer need not accept.

work.text: Now evaluate the work against its apparent project: a quiet still life is judged as a still life, not for failing to be a political mural.

taste.text: Preference is where critique starts, not where it lands — claims must point at observable features.

config.why: The work speaks, not the artist's stated intention — and the work is judged against its own project, which is the fairness principle.

activities.anchor: work on the wall, structured response, patterns named
activities.caption: match the crit format to what it trains
activities.name: critFmtMatch

config.prompt: Four professional crit formats — match format to what it trains:

pairs.right: weekly, all work visible — where vocabulary meets nerve
depth over breadth — the tutor models the grammar, not taste
the discipline of specificity without a face to read
rotating facilitation — running the room teaches as much as speaking in it

config.why: A well-run crit evaluates the journey's logic: does this exploration follow from that research? was the abandoned branch abandoned for a reason? where does the through-line break?

activities.anchor: forced to inventory what is actually on the canvas
activities.caption: fill the Feldman movements' discipline
activities.name: critFeldCloze

config.text: Feldman's movements constrain each other: describe what is literally there; analyse how the parts relate; interpret on a %%0%%, held loosely; judge %%1%%, not asserted.
config.hint: Interpretation is provisional; judgement has to be made as a case.

activities.anchor: only one of them can be wrong
activities.caption: true or false — opinion and critique
activities.name: critOpJudge

statements.s: Critique is just opinion, so everyone's opinion counts equally.
statements.why: Opinions are equally held, not equally useful — a critique is judged by whether its claims point at observable features and survive testing.

statements.s: 'I like it' and 'the diagonal leads but the colour temperature splits the focal point' are both opinions — only the specific one can be tested, which is what makes it valuable.
statements.why: Testability is what separates a critique from a verdict.

statements.s: A specific critique is falsifiable: crop it, re-tone it, and the judgement can move.
statements.why: Falsifiability is the whole point — specificity is the difference between an opinion and a critique.

activities.anchor: the only person who has seen
activities.caption: in the room vs afterwards
activities.name: critNotesSort

items.label: ask clarifying questions instead of rebutting
apply a cooling-off delay before deciding anything
act on roughly a fifth to a third of the notes
sort notes into act now, watch for, reject — with a one-line reason each

config.why: Critiques contain noise alongside signal — preferences, the critiquer's own style, contradictions — and the artist is the only person who has seen all the work; the one-line reasons are your style becoming articulate.

activities.caption: one line of this submission checklist is wrong
activities.name: critSubSpot

config.prompt: One line of this submission checklist is wrong — click it:
lines: Lead with the strongest image — the jury reads seconds per image in first passes.
Curate the selection to the portfolio's through-line.
Follow the open call's brief exactly.
Keep the artist statement vague and mystical — 'exploring the liminal' lets viewers project their own meaning.
Present materials, scale and process honestly — no misleading photographs of pieces that do not match the images.
config.correction: Positioning, not poetry: vague mysticism reads as evasion, while concrete specifics — 'paintings of decommissioned Midlands cooling towers, in the palette of their warning lights' — read as a practice.
config.why: Acceptance rates in the single digits make submissions a numbers-and-fit game — volume with consistent vision beats one perfect submission — and the duty of accuracy runs through all of it.

activities.caption: the ecosystem before / after the platform
activities.name: critEcoCompare

config.prompt: The discourse's waters — drag the divider:

before.label: the institutional frame
before.text: galleries mount curatorial arguments, fairs keep the market's calendar heartbeat, museums and biennales decide what enters the permanent story, the art press converts work into discourse

after.label: plus the platforms
after.text: Instagram flattens scale and rewards legibility-at-scroll — the ecosystem now decides what gets seen, priced and remembered at the speed of a feed

config.why: Institutional theory (Danto, Dickie): much of what makes an object 'art' is its position in the conversational apparatus — the ecosystem is part of the game, not the weather around it.
